text: R2 shipped nine reasons, not the four the spec named. The four were ready, quota_exhausted, insufficient_balance and provider_unavailable; node 1 added authentication_failed, credentials_missing, model_not_supported, invalid_output and unknown. Reviewed the widening at 9fc4a491: insufficient_balance and quota_exhausted both return before the new branch, so the generalised 'if (classified) return classified' adds only the new reasons and re-routes no existing one, and credentials_missing is matched last in classifyAvailabilityText for the same reason. unknown is the honest verdict for a probe that timed out naming no cause -- the case the spec's four could not express, and the one that bit me: the agy preflight failed at 15 seconds while the real cause, no configuration directory, was visible only on the filesystem. The spec stays as authored; this note is the reconciliation.

My packet for node 2 declared writeFiles src/engine/run-identity.mjs and test/engine/live-gate.test.mjs. Attempt 1 added a live field to the events.jsonl evidence shape, and test/campaign/field-ownership.test.mjs refused it: 'events.jsonl field(s) the document omits: [live]'. The remedy is docs/FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md, which the packet does not let it write, so the node can only pass by removing the field. That is my authoring error against a rule I wrote into AGENTS.md myself. The product question it exposes: scope closure follows syntactic edges -- imports, symbols, directory, cross-node -- and a documentation ratchet is a semantic edge it cannot see. But this one is mechanical: a packet that writes a module which appends to events.jsonl forces docs/FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md, exactly as an added schema field forces its validator. A fifth detector could refuse it at contract validate instead of at revision two, and the same shape likely covers COMMANDS.md and the source-shape ratchets.

Diagnosed all three failures of node 2 attempt 1 from the verification logs. One is in scope and two are not, so the node is expected to exhaust at maxRevisions 1. (1) test/host/preflight.test.mjs:194 -- a failed preflight dispatched the node anyway, actual running expected pending. The gate stopped refusing, the opposite of the requirement, and run-identity.mjs is in the packet so this one is fixable. (2) shared verification -- the evidence object gained a live key and env-preflight.json is spread into appendJsonl on events.jsonl at run-identity.mjs:473, so field-ownership derives live as a real events.jsonl field. The ratchet is right; docs/FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md is the remedy and is not in writeFiles. (3) test/harnesses/replay-run.test.mjs -- measured on main at 693c7a7 it passes 22 of 22 in 67.7s, and under the change it failed at 68.3s. replay-run calls runContract, which calls assertEnvironmentReady at scheduler.mjs:318, so the live ask now fires for every contract built on fixture runtimes. That is the requirement's real blast radius, not a scope miss: making the gate ask means every test that constructs a contract must have a fixture that answers. The relaunch must decide that explicitly rather than discover it at revision two.

Reproduced the replay failure in the sealed attempt-1 worktree and it names itself: env_preflight_failed: runtime luna did not answer: unknown. replay-run builds a contract on the fixture runtime luna, the gate asks it, the fixture emits a recorded worker result rather than a liveness answer, and the run is blocked before it starts. The reason is unknown, which is node 1's new honest verdict working exactly as intended. So the requirement's cost is now precise and is not a bug: once the gate asks, every test that builds a contract needs a fixture that can answer. The remedy belongs in test/helpers.mjs, which already writes the fake executables and only needs them to respond to the probe -- not in a test-mode bypass inside the gate, which would make the gate lie in exactly the way this campaign exists to stop. writeFiles for the relaunch is therefore src/engine/run-identity.mjs, test/engine/live-gate.test.mjs, docs/FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md and test/helpers.mjs. helpers is widely imported, but the AGENTS.md scope rule is about declaring a widely-imported symbol, not a widely-imported file, so symbols stays limited to names the node introduces.

I was wrong, and the worker's answer is better than the one I designed. I concluded that once the gate asks, every test building a contract needs a fixture that can answer, and I had authored a relaunch contract putting test/helpers.mjs in writeFiles to teach the fakes to respond. The real root cause of two of the three failures was one missing await: assertEnvironmentReady became async, scheduler.mjs:318 still called it synchronously, so the refusal floated off as an unhandled rejection while nodes dispatched. That is exactly what both failures said out loud and I read past it -- preflight.test.mjs reported expected pending actual running, and replay-run reported asynchronous activity after the test ended that triggered an unhandledRejection. The fix is await at the call site, and scheduler.mjs is the file my packet should have declared, by the same writeFiles rule I wrote into AGENTS.md: an async signature forces its callers. The replay case is then handled by runHasNothingToDispatch, which skips the ask when every persisted node state is done, on the principled ground that such a launch starts no worker and no judge and can spend no availability -- a real exemption that holds in production, not a test-mode bypass. And the events.jsonl field went away by writing the seven fields explicitly instead of spreading the evidence object, so live stays in env-preflight.json where it belongs and FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md needed no change. The 1b contract I prepared is discarded.

Phase 1 is not landable as it stands. Transplanted both nodes onto main at 2b7f45e and ran the suites the nodes never verified. test/run/operations.test.mjs passes 11 of 11 without the change and fails with it: env_preflight_failed: runtime luna did not answer: provider_error, thrown from assertEnvironmentReady through driveRun. Other tests in the same file pass, so this is not every fixture. The one that fails is the scope-failure test, whose fixture is deliberately rigged to produce a bad worker result. The gate now asks that same executable before the run and reads its staged work failure as a liveness failure, because liveFailureCause turns any unrecognised code into provider_error. The fixture is an inaccurate emulation and that is the finding: a real provider whose worker emits a scope violation still answers hello perfectly well. Conflating this provider is broken with this worker output is bad is the exact distinction this campaign exists to draw, and the fixtures cannot draw it because one executable answers both questions. So the remedy is on the fixture side after all, but only for the rigged-failure fixtures, and for a reason I did not have earlier. Blast radius across test/campaign/ and test/engine/ is being measured before deciding whether this is a follow-up node or an in-session fix.

Measured the full blast radius on top of main at 2b7f45e: test/engine/ 56 failures of 385, test/run/ 2 of 78, test/cli/ 1 of 111, test/campaign/ clean. Fifty-nine failures, and they are not fixture noise -- they are the tests telling me R1's blocking rule is wrong. Two shapes. First, about fifteen quota and tier exhaustion tests: the gate asks, hears exhausted, and blocks the run, so the declared failover edge is never exercised. That is worse behaviour in production too, because a contract declares a fallback precisely so the run proceeds; the gate must block only when a node has no answering runtime among its declared candidates, not when its first choice is out of quota. Second, several tests now take 61 seconds each because a silent fixture makes the gate wait out its whole 60-second budget before refusing, and the suite launches hundreds of times. So R1 lands wrong in two ways and neither is a test's fault. R2 is independent, additive and clean, so it can land alone. R1 goes back as a phase with the refined rule: the gate asks every routed runtime, and refuses only a node left with no runtime that answered.

Facts for phase 3, gathered 2026-09-22 while 1b runs. R5 has two subjects and they are in opposite states. models is already correct: its first line reads 'availability: declared catalogue only; live availability is doctors report (--probe adds per-runtime reachability)', which is exactly the requirement -- it names what it did not check. doctor is the gap, and precisely: with a contract it calls probeRuntime per routed runtime at src/host/preflight.mjs:456 and reports 'harness <id>: ok', but probeRuntime is a version check, not a live ask -- preflightContract is the live ask -- so ok there means the binary answered --version. That is the badge the campaign exists to stop reporting as a verdict. Without a contract doctor is already honest: 'no contract.json provided; skipping runtime probes'. So R5 is one change in one place: doctor either asks, or says that a version is all it verified. R4 is not spec-ready yet because plan asking first is structurally the same gate 1b is building, and specifying it before 1b settles would pin a design that may still move. This is the fifth time in this campaign that verifying found the piece already built -- isRuntimeAvailable, the freshness window, the cause classifier, runHasNothingToDispatch, and now models. The recurring lesson is to read the surface before specifying its absence.

The 1b node blocked with context_missing and it was right to. It found a contradiction my packet could not resolve and proved it rather than guessing: tier-exhaustion.test.mjs and failover.test.mjs define provider fixtures that log every invocation and assert exact contents (evidence entries exactly a,b,c at line 181; requests.length === 3 and continuationIds deep-equal for six phase tests), so a live ask adds a spawn to those logs and breaks them regardless of the blocking rule, the hello recognition, or anything else. It verified empirically that the probe request lands in such a wrapper log. My non-goal forbade editing any test, which forbade exactly the change needed. Two decisions follow. First, and this is the worker's rule, not mine, and it is better: answered means answered, not healthy. Any provider verdict counts -- a quota refusal is a hello that came back -- and only pipeline silence blocks: preflight_timeout, spawn_error, command_invalid, reported as unknown. That is the campaign's own claim stated exactly, and it dissolves the candidate-set machinery I had designed: no synthesizedChain, no failover graph, no declared-fallback reasoning, because an exhausted runtime answered. It also overturns my earlier instruction that the exhausted fixture must not answer the hello -- under this rule it must, and review.test.mjs marks a silent provider stalled forces the silent mode to answer too. Second, the two logging fixtures may be edited, narrowly: their invocation logs must ignore the hello and must keep asserting exactly what they assert today about dispatch. That is not editing a test to make it pass; it is a test whose premise -- only dispatch invokes the provider -- this requirement deliberately changes.

Sharpened R5 while 1c runs. All three surfaces use probeRuntime, which is a version check, not the live ask -- preflightContract is the live ask. Two of the three already say so about themselves: models without --probe prints 'declared catalogue only', and models --probe prints 'probed per runtime (executable reachability only)'. Both then add that doctor remains authoritative, and doctor is the one that does not. It calls probeRuntime per routed runtime at src/host/preflight.mjs:456 and reports 'harness <id>: ok' with detail 'ok', which is a version string having parsed. So the gap is not that a surface is silent about its limits; it is that the two honest ones point at the third as the authority, and the third claims an authority it does not exercise. That makes doctor the only change R5 needs, and it also means saying 'I only checked the version' is not quite enough: the other two would then defer to a command that has declared itself non-authoritative. The honest resolution is for doctor to actually ask, reusing whatever 1c lands, which is why this waits for 1c rather than going in now. Without a contract doctor is already correct: 'no contract.json provided; skipping runtime probes'.

1c is close. Nine of its eleven verification commands passed, including the two that mattered: live-gate plus preflight, and tier-exhaustion plus failover plus review -- the suites that carried about fifteen of the first attempt's 59 failures. Engine groups one through three passed too. So the rule 'only silence blocks' is the right rule and the fixture edits held. The one failure is the shared verification and it is small: the worker extracted a blockRun(runDir, evidence, blocking) helper for the three near-identical refusal paths, which is reasonable code, but docs/FIELD-OWNERSHIP.md records that events.jsonl schemaVersion is written by appendTransitionEvent and assertEnvironmentReady, and the derivation now reads blockRun. The remedy is inside run-identity.mjs, which is in the node's write scope, so this is revisable rather than blocking. Worth recording for the retrospective: the field-ownership ratchet does not only catch a new undocumented field, it catches ownership moving when a helper is extracted. Single writer per field means the writer's name is part of the contract, so a refactor that relocates an appendJsonl call is a documentation change whether or not the author thinks of it as one. That is a second way this ratchet reaches past what a packet's writeFiles anticipates, after the first attempt's undocumented live field.

My own tripwire fired and the answer is that my hypothesis was wrong, not the rule. I had written: if you need a third fixture file, stop, that means the rule is wrong again. The node stopped, correctly, at exactly three more -- routing.test.mjs flaky provider keys failures on call count and the hello consumes call 1; seal-before-kill.test.mjs hangs on call 1 by design and the hello becomes that hang, so the probe times out at 60s and the gate blocks a run the test expects to dispatch; spend.test.mjs logs every worker prompt and gains two hello entries. But it also said the thing that decides it: no failing test shows a refusal being blocked. The blocking rule is untouched. What five files show is not a wrong rule, it is a requirement that changes a global premise -- a provider is invoked only when a node dispatches -- which after R1 is simply false. Every fixture that counts or sequences invocations must distinguish the hello, exactly as fakeCodex already distinguishes a judge prompt from a work prompt. Three kinds instead of two is the same discipline, not a hack. So the tripwire was calibrated on the wrong question: the right question is not how many files need the edit, it is whether any failing test contradicts the rule. None does. Attempt 2 also fixed the field-ownership drift by moving the append back inside assertEnvironmentReady, and reached 144 of 148 on the engine batch with everything else green: field-ownership 18/18, live-gate 25/25, tier-exhaustion plus failover plus review 55/55, typecheck clean.

One more defect the suite found after the fixtures were done, and it is a real one rather than a test artefact. assertEnvironmentReady hands preflightContract the path of runDir/contract.json, and preflightContract revalidated it in full. A run launched with --base-ref was validated against the ref, whose declared paths need not exist in the working tree, so revalidating against the checkout refused it with readFiles[0] does not exist: produced.txt. In production that means the gate rejects every --base-ref launch. Fixed by giving preflightContract a persisted option and passing it from the gate: the run's own serialized contract was validated when it was authored, so re-running the filesystem-dependent checks is not a second opinion, it is a different question. The precedent was already in the same module -- line 282 reads another contract with persisted true for the same reason. The CLI's own preflight verb deliberately leaves it off, because there the contract is an authored file the operator is asking about and validating it whole is part of the answer. Worth noting for the retrospective: this is the third distinct thing the gate broke that no amount of reading would have found -- the unawaited async, the invocation counting, and now revalidation losing the launch's base ref. Each was found by a test that existed, and none by review.

CI caught what my local suite could not, because I never ran evals/. Three deterministic evals failed: D04, D07 and D12, each with 'no runtime answered the live preflight: replay-backup (cause unknown)' or replay-judge. The cause is a conceptual error of mine, not a convenience. I had put command_invalid in the set of causes that count as silence. The replay adapter throws when a runtime has no config replay.recording, and those evals declare a fallback and a judge they deliberately never invoke, so those runtimes carry no recording. The gate then blocked a run over a runtime it would never have used, on a fault the provider never had. A command that could not be constructed never reached a provider: the gate learned nothing about availability and has no verdict to report, and an unbuildable runtime command is a contract defect that validation already owns. So LIVE_SILENCE_CAUSES is now preflight_timeout and spawn_error only -- asked and said nothing, or could not be started to be asked. Evals went 14/17 to 17/17 and live-gate plus preflight stayed 25/25, so the distinction did not loosen the gate. Second lesson, and it is the same one for the third time: my verification did not cover where the code runs. evals/ is a whole surface my mirror-coverage detector cannot see either, because it maps src/<layer> to test/<layer> and evals/ is neither.

Phase 1 landed. R2 as 13094e0 and R1 as b489e8c. The gate asks every routed runtime one trivial prompt before any dispatch and blocks only a provider that was asked and said nothing; the verdict names six failure causes plus ready and unknown. It took three launches and every one failed for a different reason, all three of them mine. The first contract's verification never touched test/engine/, where the code it changed lives, so 56 failures of 385 were invisible to the gate that certified it -- now a contract-validation warning, landed as 8c26c95. The second spec blocked whenever any routed runtime failed to answer, which refused runs their declared fallback existed to carry; the executing node stopped and returned the better rule, that answered means answered and not healthy. The third packet's writeFiles did not reach the fixtures that count provider invocations, and six of them needed to learn that the hello is not a dispatched turn -- now a rule in AGENTS.md. After all that, CI still found one more: command_invalid counted as silence, so a fallback runtime that was declared but never invoked could block a whole run. Three defects here were found by tests that already existed and none by review: the unawaited async gate, the invocation counting, and revalidation losing the launch's base ref.

Found while preparing the close, and the irony is exact. buildRequirementClosure credits a requirement to any node that reached done carrying its id. R1 will therefore record as closed by the-dispatch-gate-asks-before-it-passes, from the first run -- the node whose work passed its judge and then broke 56 of 385 engine tests, and which I did not land. What shipped as R1 came from the 1c node, which blocked with context_missing and never reached done, plus four fixture edits and the --base-ref fix I made myself. So the closure record attests that a node with that requirement id reached done. It does not attest that the requirement was delivered, and in this case those are two different pieces of work by two different nodes. That is a badge, not a verdict, in a campaign whose entire subject is the difference. I am not proposing to fake the record -- it says what happened and should. The question for a later campaign is whether closure should be keyed on what landed on the integration branch rather than on what passed a gate, since the two can diverge and here they did.

The R4 node blocked with context_missing and it found a contradiction I had written into its packet. liveSilenceCause and LIVE_SILENCE_CAUSES are module-private to run-identity.mjs, which the packet forbade changing, so a refusal in plan/ could only duplicate them -- and a duplicate top-level body trips source-shape. The packet demanded the gate's exact discipline and forbade the only way to reuse it. It also asked the right question about reachability, which I answered myself rather than paying another hour. reachableRuntimes at host/preflight.mjs adds the judge role only when a node gate is enabled, and plan/template.mjs builds every planning contract with gate false. So the reviewer is never a judge in a planning contract: it is the worker of the review stage's own contract, built later. One preflightContract call on the draft contract therefore reaches the planner and never the reviewer, exactly as the node suspected, and that is precisely why a mute reviewer surfaced only after the draft had been bought. The design that follows: preflightContract now delegates to a new preflightRuntimes that takes runtime entries rather than a contract -- one asking function with two entry points, so no caller can accidentally ask a different question -- liveSilenceCause is exported so planning and dispatch cannot drift on what silence is, and src/plan/preflight.mjs asks both roles before the first stage. It lives beside pipeline.mjs because that file is 45 lines from the 800 ceiling and because asking is its own concern. I implemented it rather than relaunching: the design was settled and this is the fourth packet-scope failure of the campaign.

R4 landed as a6a5d43. Planning now asks both the runtimes it will spend before its first stage, and refuses on the dispatch gate's own silence rule rather than a copy of it. The design fact that made it precise: plan/template.mjs builds every planning contract with gate false, and reachableRuntimes only counts the judge role when a node's gate is enabled, so the reviewer is never a judge in a planning contract -- it is the worker of the review stage's own contract, built after the draft has been bought. That is why preflighting the draft contract could never have reached it, and why the ask had to name the runtimes directly. preflightContract now delegates to preflightRuntimes: one asking function with two entry points, so the probe, the throwaway repository, the budget and the detail wording stay decided in one place. liveSilenceCause is exported so planning and dispatch cannot drift on what silence is. Four of five requirements are on main. One note on the CI: the Windows job that arrived with 87069e7 from another session is flaky -- on the same main commit, windows 24 passed while windows 22 failed, which is flake by definition, and the R4 PR went green on a rerun with no code change. Not this campaign's defect, but whoever owns that job should know.

Ford relayed an external audit's review of faberun 0.18.0 from an independent session on another repository. I verified all four findings against main myself rather than taking the report on faith, and all four hold. (1) A judge finding below failOn vanishes: render.mjs:474 gates the findings report on node.status === exhausted, so a node that reached done carrying a real fail verdict shows nothing, and MAX_NOTE_LENGTH at render.mjs:600 is 64 characters, which is where the note gets cut. The gate passing is correct and documented at render.mjs:148 -- that is what failOn means -- but the finding then becomes unreadable. (2) spec validate never runs a proof: plan/spec.mjs:307 checks presence only. This one touches me directly. I ran spec validate --strict-traceability on all four phase specs this session and it told me nothing about whether their proofs pass; they do, but only because I ran them by hand. (3) maxTurns default 150 at contract/index.mjs:53 appears only in docs/VISION.md:60 and is absent from references/contract.md. One correction to the reviewer's P0: per-node maxTurns already exists -- contract/index.mjs:41 lists it, :243 validates it, process.mjs:452 reads job.node?.maxTurns ?? contract.maxTurns -- so the adjustability half is built and only the documentation and the 80% warning are missing. (4) final.mjs:63 and :112 read node.runtime, which after a judge phase is the judge, while render.mjs:84 reads workerRuntime ?? runtime and is right. workerRuntimeLabel already exists at render.mjs:573, one module away and unused by final.mjs. That is the same shape as the signal-block defect I fixed this morning: one rule, two readers, the incomplete one on the path that mattered. None of the four overlaps R1-R5; that campaign was about the verdict, this one is about the operator seeing it. They are the same thesis one level up -- the tool knows and the operator does not see -- and my own requirement-closure-is-itself-a-badge finding from this morning belongs with them as a fifth.

Integrating R5 found two defects before it landed, both of the same family the campaign is about. The node had written a second copy of the silence rule with command_invalid in it -- the one the gate deliberately dropped after three deterministic evals showed it blocks a run over a runtime it would never have used. It could not have known: its base predates R4 exporting the rule. And my own fix for that, importing from run-identity.mjs, closed a runtime import cycle, because doctor owns reachableRuntimes which live-preflight imports. source-shape caught it and its assertion message said what to do. So the rule now lives in src/engine/live-silence.mjs with all three readers importing it. R4's export was the right instinct and the wrong shape: it worked for two readers and broke on the third. Worth naming for the next campaign: the repo has a ratchet that catches a rule with divergent readers in src/, and that ratchet is exactly what the external review's fourth finding is about -- report.json reading node.runtime while STATUS reads workerRuntime -- except across report surfaces, where no ratchet exists. Same defect class, one side mechanically guarded and the other not.

Five requirements delivered: the verdict names six failure causes (13094e0), the dispatch gate asks every routed runtime and blocks only silence (b489e8c), a verdict is persisted and reused inside a 15-minute window the hello owns (68c3e87), planning asks both its roles before the first stage (a6a5d43), and doctor reports the verdict instead of a version (6d91146). The work was small -- R1 was about 150 lines across three files, the campaign cost about two dollars -- and the wall clock was almost entirely my authoring. One mistake three times: a node's verification did not cover where its code runs. The first contract verified for three minutes, passed its judge, and broke 56 of 385 tests in the directory holding the module it changed; the fixtures that count provider invocations were outside the write scope; and a locally green suite went red in CI on evals/. Two guards landed for it: 8c26c95 warns when a node writes src/<layer>/ and nothing runs a test under test/<layer>/ that the contract does not itself write, and AGENTS.md carries the fixture rule with all six files named. Workers corrected my design twice and both times were right: 'answered means answered, not healthy' came from a node that stopped rather than implement my worse rule, and it retired an entire candidate-set machinery. Three defects were found by tests that already existed and none by review: the async gate its caller did not await, revalidation losing the launch's base ref, and command_invalid classified as silence. What I would do differently: prototype the seam and run the suite before authoring. Phase 1b's spec carried a measured failure baseline and the next launch reached 144 of 148 first try; phase 1's carried none and failed entirely. Same machine, same models. One honest note: the closure record credits R1 to the node that reached done, not to the work that shipped, which came from a node that blocked plus fixes I made myself. In a campaign about badges and verdicts, the closure record is a badge.
